headline: THE CITY.

text:
ONE!-The hour, solitary in It's sound


lonely in its melody, solemn in its gloomy
singleness, resounds in dull and dreamy
emphasis over the city, and reaches the
wanderer in the remotest corner of the
town. ONE-prefaced by a merry jingle
from the old clock on the Catholic Church
breaks through the still atmosphere upon
the ear like the voice of some gloomy spir-
it who dwels in the steeple. ONE!-the
clock has just struck, says the Citizen of the
World, the expiring taper rises and sinks
in the socket, the watchman forgets the
hour in slumber, the laborious and the hap
py are at rest, and nothing wakes but med
itation, guilt, revelry and despair. The
drunkard once more fills the destroying,
bowl, the robber walks his midnight round,
the ruined gambler stakes his last dollar on
the card, the suicide lifts his guilty hand
against his own person.


Let ME no longer waste the night over
the page of history, or the sallies of con-
temporary genius, but pursue the solitary
walk, where Vanity, ever changing, but a
few hours past walked before, where she
kept up the pageant, and now, like fro
ward child, seems hushed with her own i'm
portunities.


What gloom hangs all around! The
flickering lamp feebly emits yellow
CLEAN; no sound Is heard but of the Ginning
clock, or the evagabond dog. All the luster
of human pride is forgotten-an hour like
this may well display the emptiness of hui
man vanity. There will come time when
this temporary solitude may be made con-
tinual, and the city itself, like its inhabi-
tants, fade away and leave desert in its
room. What cities, as great and greater
than this, have once triumphed in exist
ence, had their victories as great joy as just
and as unbounded, and with short sighted
presumption, promised themselves immor-
tality. Posterity can hardly trace the sit
uation of some, the sorrowful traveller wan
ders over the awful ruins Of others, and as
he beholds he learns wisdom and feels the
transciencc of every earthly possession.-
The citadel is now ovcrgrown with
weeds; their senate houses now the haunt
of noXious reptiles; their temples and the
aters now one common heap OF ruins.


How few appear in those streets which
but few hours ago were crowded! and
those who appear now no longer wear their
daily mask, nor attempt to hide their lcwd-
ness or their misery. But who are those
who make the streets their couch, and find
Il short repose from wretchcdness at the
doors of strangers? These are strangers,
orphans and wanderers, whose circum-
stances are too humble for redress, and
whose distresses are too great even for pity.
Their wretchedness excites horror rather
than pity. Poor shivering females, once
knowing happier days, now covered with
rags, cmaciated with disease: the world has
disclaimed them; society turns its back up
on their misery, and has given them up to
nakedness, hunger and despair Prostitut-
ed to the gay, luxurious villain, they are
perhaps now prowling about the haunts of
their betrayers and sue to wretches whose
hearts are insensible, or debauchees who
may curse but will not relieve
them. These miserablcs may weep
unheeded, prosecuted by every subor-
dinate species of tyranny; and every
law which gives Others security becomes
an enemy to them. Why is the heart
formed with so much sensibility, when the
fortune is not adapted to its impulses. Gen
erosity, without capacity for relieving,
only makes the man who feels it more
wretched than the object which sues for ex-
istence. .r..


But let us turn from scene of such dis
tres to the sanctifed hypocrite, who has
been talking of virtue till the time of bed,
and now steals out to give loose to his
vices under the protection of midnight;
vices more atrocious because he attempts to
conceal them. See how lie pants down the
dark alley; and with fastening steps, fears
an acquaintance in every face. He has pass
ed the day in company he hates, and now
goes to prolong the night among company
that as heartily hate him. May his vices be
detected, and may the morning rise upon
his shame! ...

ton.

New YORK, June 3.-The Herald's Fifth


corps correspondent says of the battle OF


Monday: At six o'clock p. M. the enemy
assaulted our line. 1t was a general and
sudden attack. They advanced in two lines
OF battle and heavy skirmish line. Sim
ultaneously with their opening volley OF
musketry, came solid shot and shell from
the mouths of a score or more of cannon.
Firm and unflinching stood our men. The
rebels shot too high-our men coolly waited
to return the llre-it was most murderous
Volley; the assaulting column were stag
gered and fell back. Our artillery, which
had been in position, opened responsive to
the enemy's cannon. Assault after assault
was made by the desperate foe, but each
time our troops hurled him back.


Upon Gen. Crawtord.s division the as
saults were repeated and frequent. The
enemy sought TO turn his left, but each time
were handsomely repulsed; and more than
special glory was won by the men meeting
and repelling these assaults. The Pennsyl-
yania Reserves behaved magnificently. In
the division and holding the extreme left,
was Gen. Lockwood and his troops, most OF
them for the first time under fire. They
behaved like veterans. Col. Kichens brig
ade of heavy artillery was on the field and
stood its ground with the resoluteness of
LILO ullSduC BIRH-
ty prisoners. The contest closed with our
having driven the enemy, as stated above
and occupying the battle ground.


Our losses were two hundred killed,
wounded and missing. Among the killed
was Maj. Elkert, commanding the 64th
Michigan regiment. The enemy's losses
are much heavier-probably fifteen hun
dred. We captured two hundred prisoners,
among them ten commissioned officers.
Among their dead is said to have been
found rebel General and two Colonies.
Prisoners all say the whole of Ewell's corps
was engaged against us; the corps, they
say, however, is commanded by Early, and
General Ewell in command of the army,
Lee being in Richmond.


A rumor has prevailed that Lee was
wounded in the leg at Spottsylvania C. III :;
but it is not authenticated. There can be
no doubt, however, that he does not COM
mand the rebel army at present.

Yesterday little after 10 o'clock the
fiercest of the late battles i'm the Wilderness
opened. 1t ragged till after dark. Part OF
Burnside's Corps was on our right, with the
9Th and 9th Corps in the center, and the I'd
on the left. Our line extended along the
north bank of the PO river while that of the
rebels was Immediately on the opposite
side, including Spottsylvania. About the
middle of the afternoon our artillery show
cred shell and grape on the enemy's lines
with terrible effect, but without checking
his stubborn resistance. The enemy
brought but little artillery into action, de-
pending chiefly on infantry charges. All
the prisoners taken during the former part
of the day were from Longstreet's and Hills
corps, which gave the impression that Ew-
ell had withdrawn, but later events proved
this erroneous. Toward evening the battle
ragged all along the line, each vieing for the
vantage ground, but neither gaining it.


Generals Grant and Meade Immediately
supervised the whole action, and were fire.
quently cheered during the heaviest firing.
About dusk it was found that the enemy
was throwing heavy columns round our
right flank, with the intention of making q
desperate effort to break through our lines
during the night and capture large
amount of our supplies, which were COM
ing up. Observing this the 9th corps
charged on his right center while Burnside
moved on his right. We drove him from
his rifle pits and captured 1000 prisoners
and several guns.


Grant now retired short distance to a
new and better position, and all night our
men rested ON their arms, but the enemy
did not advance, which led to the belief
that he was severely punished, as he had a
decided advantage in the evening.


Our own losses in this days fight were
very heavy, and principally in wounded
The long marches and continued series of
battles are wearing on our men, but not
subduing their courage.

text:
New ORLEANS, July 3O.-Information
was received at headquarters Department
of the Gulf Thursday, that Admiral Farra-
gut had passed forts Morgan and Gaines,
which had been supposed to command the
entrance to Mobile bay. and is bombardng
the upper defenses. If this information is
correct, the forts must speedily surrender.
The Admiral has now six ironclads off Mo-
bile, and two more left this city to-day.
The ebombardmentha has continued three days,
and it is expected the city will surrender
before the close of the next week. Gen.
Granger will command the land forces
which will occupy Mobile and garrison the
forts, if perfect success crowns the move
ments of Admiral Farragut, as everybody
here expects.


On the 10th Of July, Gen. Asboth, COM
manding at Pensacola, left that post with a
small force, and the next day came upon a
body of the enemy's cavalry, about four
hundred strong, strongly entrenched at
Fort Hobson. After sharp fight the reb-
els retreated, leaving all their ammunition,
their flag, official papers, stores, seventeen
horses, &c. Gen. Asboth then returned to
Pensacola.


Our forces have evacuated Brownsville,
Texas, and all the stores have been sent to
Brazos and New Orleans.

LOUISVILLE, Dec. 3.-The Journal con-
tains the following special The enemy
has been wary to-day, and has demonstra-
ted with great caution against our line,
which Is carefully constructed and extends
from river to river with radius Of two and
half miles from the capitol, on the roads
south of the city. The enemy's cavalry

been developed. Some artillery firing oc-

shots were fired. The defenses are being
hourly strengthened and no apprehensions
need be felt for the safety of the city.

New YORK, Nov. 25.-Ihe Herald's dis
patches from the Shenandoah Valley say
that Gen. Sheridan's cavalry have had an
other very brilliant and successful engage
ment with Early's army. On Monday last
three divisions of Union cavalry in the Val
ley, under Custar, Powell and Devin, COM
menced movement for the purpose OF as
certaining the rebel position and strength.
Devin marched up the Luray Valley and
the two other divisions pushed up the She
nandoah Valley, driving before them small
parties of rebels. No resistance of impor-
tance was met with till Tuesday. The main
infantry army, consisting of about 1900
men, and division of cavalry, were found
at Rood's Hill, position almost as strong
as Fishers Hill. Fighting Immediately COM
menced andp was continued tor six hours,
which was during the greater part of the
time quite severe. Early made repeated at
tempts TO flank Custar and Powell, in all of
which he failed. Some magnificent charges
were made by the Union cavalry. The
rebels showed little spirit during the en-
gagement.


After gaining sufficient information of
Early's strength, objects and position, the
national forces commenced to retire. Some
feeble attempts to follow and annoy were
made but without any success to the enc
my, and Custar and Powell returned down
the valley with their command in safety,
having lost altogether in killed, wounded
and missing only about sixty men.


The dispatches furnish confirmation of
the report that some Of Early's men have
been Withdrawn from the valley, but the
rebels say they have been replaced by scat
tered detachments fran various sections.

THE FIGHTING BEFORE ATLANTA.


The fights leave our army unbroken in
strength and spirits, and ready to move for
ward whenever their gallant chief shall
give the word. Our wounded are well cared
for, and bear their misfortunes like heroes
Seldom is complaint heard in the hospi-
tai.


The general impression there is that our
entire loss in the recent battles will not
amount to more than 5000. The loss ofthe
enemy in killed and wounded has also been
overrated, as they fought, for the most part,
behind entrenchments.


The movement of Hardee against the en-
emy's left wing was one of the most dash
ing of the war, and a complete surprise.
His men dashed upon the enemy as storm
from the clouds, and so panic-stricken were
the vandals that the first line threw down
their arms and ran toward our lines, shout
ing at the top of their voices, "Don't shoot;
we surrender" The prisoners sent to the
rear, Hardee attacked the second line and
carried it, but with considerable loss to his
corps. He held their works for more than
day, no serious effort being made to mo-
lest him, and then moved to more fruit
full portion of the field. r1,


The enemy have some heavy Parrott
guns posted on the hills about three miles
southwest of the city, from which they con-
tinue day and night to throw shells into the
town, but without serious damage. They
have thus far showed but little desire to re-
new the fight. a -.

About eight o'clock yesterday morning
fire broke out in the collection Of shanties
on Water street in the rear of the Gas Fac
tory, known as Smiths Row "a name as
familiar to the Police Court and City Prison
as household words, and connected with
every species and denomination of petty
offenses and minor crimes. The architectu-
raj arrangement of the "Row" is a novelty
in Itself. There are perhaps fifteen differ
ent shanties, the oldest one having been
built twenty years ago, the others,
seeming to be the progeny OF, lean
crafty on the first. There are shanties
with porches, and shanties withoutporches;
with shutters and without; with windows
and with holes. Fifty chimneys peep out
from fifty different corners, and blacken
with their fifty different smokes the face of
the huts; fifty different smells from fifty
different kinds of filth rise up from the hol-
low in which the Row reposes, to smite the
sense of the intruder and fifty kinds of
oaths in dozen languages, may be heard



The doors hang upon one hinge, the shut
ters lean tipsily against each other; and
each window, filled with old hats or old
clothes, seems about to fall into its neigh
Dor which is similarly ornamented. There
are cellars protected by rotten door-ways,
through which man could tumble into the
midst of family group at any time; and
there are rickety stairways leading no one
knows where, looking as if they had a
spite against mankind and were only wait
ing favorable opportunity to fall upon
and crush somebody. Passing under an
arch freshly painted with dazzling blue,
one will find court with a huge dungheap
in the centre, around which are collected o
new installment of tenements invisible
from the outside; and in this court children,
hogs, dogs, and cows revel in one promis-
cuous fellowship. There are perhaps thirty
families occupying the Row and each family
is supplied with half dozen children, from
the nursing babe to the toddling urchin,
the vicious looking boy and the dirty faced
girl. Over and about all these hangs an air
of indescribable dilapidation, squallidness,
misery, poverty, filth and horror, which to
be appreciated must be seen.


An alarm of fire in such place created
the utmost CONSERVATION, and occasioned q
scene which Hogarth might have painted,
but no one can describe. Each family be-
gan to provide against the devouring ele-
ment by tunbling their household goods in
the street, commencing with the babies.
They were piled in a heap, and while their
half naked mothers were dragging out the
furniture, the little ones sprawled about in
the dirt, confounding confusion by their
cries. The babies cried, the men cursed,
the women screamed and the dogs threw in
q dismal chorus of howls. Stoves were car
ried out and set down upon the toes of by
ISLANDERS; clocks were pitched into the
street and smashed; and women, half stu
pefied with smoke and whisky, were dragged
out by the heels.


When the steam fire engines arrived and
began pouring tremendous streams of wa
ter through the windows, doors and crew.
ces in the burning shanties the confusion
reached its height. The denizens of the
place ran about like mad people, and many
of them received more cold water than they
had been acquainted with for years. One
woman was knocked down stairs by a
stream of water with which she collided.
Another female, toothless, bare headed,
drunk and horrible, rushed frantically
among the crowd talking wildly in glib
berish which no one could understand; and
an old woman, who had lost her wig in the
melee, lit her pipe with spark, and sit
ting down upon heap of furniture, calm
ly surveyed the scene before her.


The engines worked away vigorously and
saved the shell of Smiths Row; but what of
household goods spared by the fire were
damaged by the water with which every
thing around was flooded. The inhabitants
ceased their bowling and began to identity
their goods-including babies-which labor
was not performed without considerable
difficulty and some fights. Before the water
ceased dripping from the caves, the bare
footed women were bailing out their cribs,
preparatory to resuming the even tenor of
that domestic felicity which had been so
unusually disturbed.

Yesterday little band of one hundred
and four soldiers, rank and file, marched
up High street from the depot to the State
House yard, escorted by Hemmersbach's
brass band, of this city. These men were
the re-enlisted veterans OF the Fifty-eighth
Ohio Infantry, who arrived from Vicksburg
to be furloughed to their homes for thirty
days. There was an impression prevailing
that the term of service of this regiment
had expired. and that this detachment was
all that was left of the regiment, but this
was erroneous, as about one hundred of the
old regiment, who did not re-enlist, are still
at Vicksburg, under Colonel Jackson, who
Is now its commanding officer. Many of
our citizens distinctly remember the regi-
ment when, little less than three wears
ago, it marched down High street one
thousand strong, and the contrast between
that splendid array and the squad which
returned, suggested itself to every mind.


The Fifty-Eighth was organized as
German Regiment and left Champ Chase
for the front under command of Col. Bau-
senwein, but was subsequently, commanded
by Col. Deister, who was killed before
Vicksburg, and is now under Col. Jackson.
No Regiment that left Ohio has had more
i'll luck or sustained severer losses than the
5Sth. At Fort Donelson it received its first
baptism of fire and blood, and in all the bat
ties from Donelson to the capture of Vicks-
burg, including the three days at Shiloh,
Sherman's attacks on Vicksburg, Arkansas
Post, it participated and suffered heavily
by rebel bullets. In ShermaE's disastrous
attempt on Vicksburg the 5Sth bore the most
conspicuous part and was nearly annihi-
lated. The regiment started over a swamp
to storm Chickasaw Bluff, with four hun
dred men, but less than one half of them
returned to their line and there were none
taken prisoners. They succeeded in reach
ing the enemy's works, but were driven
back from the muzzle of the rebel guns,
lelving the most of the officers and
men with which they started. Here fell
the solderly and gallant Col. Deister, on
the parapet of the works crying, Forward
Fifty-eighth !" Here fell the noble, chival-
rous, ,simp1e-hearted Captain Kaufman, than
whom no more heroic soldier or better
man ever went down in battle; here fell the
Lieutenant-Colonel, Major, and Captains
and subalterns in terrible profusion. After
this dreadful slaughter they could not mus
ter men enough to make regiment and
the remaining men were placed on gum
boats and the officers accepted staff ap-
pointments or came home disabled. Since
active operations ceased, however, they
were recognized, and have since been sta
toned at Vicksburg. Now, just one-half
of what is left of the old ten hundred come
home to enjoy thirty days of rest, after an
experience which has rarely had its parallel
even in the history of these times of mel
ancholy wonders and manifold disasters by
flood and field.

Almost everybody has heard Of the walking
leaves Of Australia. For a long time after the
discovery of that island many people really be.
leyed that the leaves of a certain tree which
fOurished there could walk about the grOund.
This story arose in this way. Some English sailors
landed upon the coast one day, and after roam
ing about until they were tired they sat down
under tree 70 rest themselves. A puff of wind
came along and blew OFF Q shower of leaves,
which after turning over and over in the air, as
leaves generally do, finally rested upon the
ground.


As il was midsummer and everything appeared
quite green, the circumstance puzzled the sailors
considerably. But their surprise was much
greater, as YOU may well suppose, when after a
short time they saw the leaves crawling along the
ground towards the trunk of the tree. They ran
at once for the vessel, without stopping 10 exam
inc into the matter &C all, and set sail from the
land where everything seemed bewitched. One
of the men said he expected every moment to
see TIE trees set 10 and dance jig"


Late explorations Of Australia have taught us
that these walking leaves are insects.


They live upon the trees. Their bodies are
very thin and fat their wings forming large leaf
like organs. When they are disturbed their legs
are folded away urder their bodies, leaving the
shape exactly like leaf with It's stem and all
complete. They are of bright dten color In
the summer, bat they gradually ciihnge in the
faA, with the caves, into the brown Of frost
bitten vegetation. When shaken from the tree.
they lie for few moments upon the GROUND as
though they were dead, but presently they begin
10 crawl along towards the tree, which they ascend
Rgain. They rarely use their wings, although
they are pretty well supplied In this respect.

and New Brunswick.

PHILADELPHIA, Dec. l2.-The Bulletin
has the following important intelligence:


The steamer Donegal arrived this after
noon from the South Atlantic blockading
squadron, having left Port Royal on the
9TH inst. The joint naval and land eXpedi-
tion under Admiral Dahlgren and General
Foster proceeded from Beaufort up the
Broad river on Tuesday, December 9th, the
object being to destroy the Pocotaligo
bridge, on the railroad between Charleston
and Savannah. The Donegal accompanied
accompany it further. There were seven
gunboats in the expedition, and soon after
reaching proper position, heavy fire was
opened by them. A force was landed and
an action commenced. Before evening
Pocotaligo bridge was reached and des-
troyed. Our troops were then intrenched
for such future operations as might be
needed.


The Donegal came down to Port Royal
the same evening, but could not bring any
details of the losses on either side. OF the
success of the grand object of the eXpedi-
ton, however, there can be no doubt. Our
informant speaks in the highest terms of
the energy and activity of Admiral Dahl
ment of the naval brigade in this affair.


When the Donegal left to come down
Broad river the evening of the 9th, shells
were seen flying and exploding, which in
dicated that our forces were determined to
drive the enemy out of any position they
might have taken after being driven from
the bridge. Gen. Fosters scouts had COM
municated with Gen. Sherman's forces,
which were marching on Savannah. The
belief was that Gen. Sherman would be In
Savannah on Wednesday, the 14th inst.


The Pocotaligo bridge is about thirty
five miles from Savannah. This bridge
having been destroyed, and Sherman hav-
ing cut the other railroad communications,
Savannah cannot be relieved by reinforce
ments from any point north of that city.

KANSAS CITY, Oct 22-The fight yester-
day between Little Blue river and Inde-
pendence was very gallant affair. We
fought Prices entire army for five hours.
McLean's Colorado battery silenced the
rebel guns, and Col. Hoyt made gallant
sabre charge with battalion of the 10Th
Kansas. The I'd Colorado lost 60 killed and
wounded; among the former, Major Smith,
commanding the regiment. Our total loss
wasover 400. We evacuated Independence,
falling back to Big Blue. Militia have ar
rived, and this morning we hold the line of
Big Blue. Generals Curtis, Blunt and Dietz-
Ter are on the ground.


About two o'clock this morning Colonel
Jennison, with the 18th Kansas and several
guns, was attacked at ByrOn's Ford by a
heavy column of the enemy, and about p.
M.the rebels forced the fore, ,Jennison falling
back toward Westport and the State line.
COL Moonlight went to his assistance
Both commands got separated from the
main force. A portion of the Kansas mill
tia fought near Bickhaw's Mills, but were
compelled to retreat, falling back to Shaw
neetown. The main body of the militia
marched to Kansas City, where headquar-
ters now are. They occupy entertainments
and are in good spirits. Colonels Jennison
and Moonlight, and Major Hunt, with
Gen. Curtis body-guard, fought the enc
my till some time after dark, driving them
four miles over an open prairie. Our loss
was inconsiderable; the rebels more than
400. We captured $50 stand of arms. and
the rebel Captain Won Volkenburg, brother
to the New York Congressman. Jennison
and Moonlight are at the State line, and
Price at Wagon Farm, moving rapidly in
three columns.


At sundown message was received from
Gen. Pleasanton, stating that he was press
ing Price with 10000 men. He had fought
them on the field of yesterday, drove them
from Independence, and was pursuing them
sharply. Price is heading for Kansas, and
may cross the State line in his retreat.


A general battle has been fought at Kan
sas City, and great victory won. Prices
whole army is reported retreating rapidly
south, with our cavalry in hot pursuit, al
together, with Pleasanton's forces, number
ing $4,000 men only. Price may strike for
Fort Scott, but will be too closely followed
to do much damage.


Pleasanton closed yesterdays battle at
Independence by capturing a large number
of prisoners and three pieces of artillery.


This morning our line formed five miles
south of Kansas City, on the Westport road.
Skirmishing continued for several hours,
when the whole force advanced and heavy
fighting ensued. The enemy rapidly fell
back and formeda a new line mile and
half from the first position. An artillery
engagement then ensued, our infantry
slowly advancing. Fighting was kept up
for ten miles from this point, the enemy
gradually falling back. Pleasanton then
came in on our left, and a grand charge
followed, resulting in the total rout of the
enemy.


When our informant left the front our
whole cavalry was in vigorous pursuit, the
infantry following. ys


Gen. Blunt commanded the volunteer
force on the left, and Gen. Deitzler the
center, composed of militia, who behaved
gallantly. The I'd Colorado (Col. Ford) was
in the thickest of the fight and made sew
eral brilliant charges. Gen. Deitzler, Gov.
Carney and Gen. Curtis were constantly
with the advance. Our loss is not heavy.
That of the rebels, from the number of
dead and wounded left on the field, must
be very great.

BALTIMORE, August 23.-The following is
published in the American this morning,
the substance OF which the censor would
not permit transmission over the wires last
night:


HARPER's FERRY, Aug. pa brisk en-
gagement occurred yesterday two miles
beyond Charlestown, between the Army of
Western Virginia and the rebel force now
in the Shenandoah Valley. The battle was
commenced by q heavy column of rebel
infantry and cavalry attempting to pierce
our front near Summit Point, and after q
sharp but decisive struggle, our skirmish-
ers were compelled to give way. The First
division of Gen. Wilson and Gen. Torbetz's
cavalry corps were engaged, and suffered
heavily. The movement had evidently for
its object the possession of Martinsburg for
time, till false movement was made
against our extreme left. But suddenly
new body of rebels appeared in front of
our right consisting of the Sixth, Eighth
and Nineteenth corps. A short but deter
mined battle took place. The Second di-
vision lost heavily-some three hundred
wounded and sixty or seventy killed and
missing. Our right drove the enemy over
a mile, and then fell back to their old line
until 10 o'clock, when the entire army re-
tired toward Halltown, where they now
are in line of battle.
HThere are rumors ahoat that the rebels
are crossing the Potomac at Martinsburg.
Certain 1t is, the rebels have possession of
Martinsburg.


Gen. McIntosh's brigade of that division
lost nearly three hundred men, but only
one officer was seriously injured. Acting
Adjutant Lloyd, 22d Wisconsin cavalry,
and three other officers, were slightly
wounded, but have not yet left their COM
mands. The Sth corps, Gen. Crook, were
only partly engaged, and lost but few men.
The left, consisting of the 9th corps, Gen.
Emery, were not engaged, as their line
rested on Berryville pike. Our entire line
extended from Berryville pike on the left
to Smithfield pike on the right, and occu-
pied the commanding line of country run
ming between these two roads, situated two
miles from Charlestown.


Our cavalry, after the enemy had shifted
his front from our lett to our right, retired
down the Berryville pike, and passing
through Charlestown, bivouacked in fields
to the right of the town. All last night
troops were passing through Charlestown
in the direction of Halltown. The cavalry
were left in front OF Charlestown and their
pickets relieved the infantry before day
light. Atsunrise forward" was sounded,
and the entire cavalry corps moved forward
and took up the position abandoned by the
9Th and 9th Corps. Our cavalry had orders
to push through to Martinsburg, and the
infantry are busy pitching impromptu
camps along their line of battle, awaiting
the result.

New YORK, July 12.-On Sunday after
noon, the steamer Electric Spark, on yoy-
age from this port to Havana and New Or
leans, was boarded and taken possession of
by the privateer Florida. When the Florida
was first discovered she was distant about
fifteen miles to the northward, and making
for the Electric Spark, which gained on her
rapidly; when seven or eight miles distant
the Florida hoisted the English flag, which
she kept flying until within twelve hundred
yards of the steamer, when the rebel colors
were substituted and shot fired astern of
the Electric Spark, closely followed by an
other across her bow. The steamer not
coming to Immediately, shell was fired,
which, after striking the water few feet
from the vessel passed directly over her
about midship. The steamer then hove to
and was Immediately boarded by a party
from the Florida, who took possession of
her and ordered her Captain on board the
privateer with his papers. All personal
property was destroyed or taken, but the
steamer with all the mails contained in six
ty-five bags was retained.


The English schooner Lave had been pre-
viously boarded by the Florida, and was
near by at tle time of the capture of the
Electric Spark. Both steamers soon head
ed for the schooner, which hove to until
they came up. The Captain, crew and pas
sengers about forty in number, were then
put on board the Lave, which was bound
for this port. The Lave arrived here last
evening.


The Electric Spark had a very narrow
escape from destruction, being mistaken
for transport. Had she not stopped after
the third shot, broadside from the rebel
battery, which was in readiness for the pur-
pose, would have destroyed here.

One of the most heart-rending casualties
that we have been called upon to record for
some time, occurred yesterday. The cir
cumstances as developed before the Coro-
ner's Jury are as follows: Yesterday
morning, about o'clock, two boys, named
George and Frank Rossman, aged IA and 8
wears, respectively, left the home of their
parents, situated on High street, in StOrrs
Township, and with their sled started for a
mornings pleasure on the ice of Millcreek.


They went forth full of merriment and
big with expectation of fine days sport.
Once upon the ice, which to all indications
appeared strong and bearable, they glided
RAPIDLY over its surface until they had
reached a distance of at least fifty feet from
the shore, when the ice gave way, and
they fell through and passed under. Their
elder brother John Fl. Rossman, aged
2l.years, with. several other citizens, were
on the c., III. and Dayton railway track,
watching the boys in their youthful glee,
and when they broke through the Ice, John
and his friends ran down; to rescue the un-
fortunate lads. The ice also broke beneath
them, and John went under, never to re-
turn Ff3e -' eew EuuEH 1Ts1 T.-


IL was with difficulty that the five citi-
zens escaped with their lives, one of them,
named John Muller, being rescued as he
was going down the last time. The water
under the Ice where the boysbroke through,
was about twelve. feet deep, and was the
back water from. the swollen Ohio, which,
falling rapidly, left about. one and half
feet vacancy between the ice and the wa
ter. The bedies of the three brothers were
recovered in about an honr after they were
drowned, and were at once conveyed to the
residence of their parents, who received
the first intimation of their death when
their bodies were brought into the house.
The heart-rending shrieks of the mother
and two sisters was terrible, while the sobs
and lamentations of the father and son ex-
cited the deepest sympathy. The coroner
held an inquest, and the jury returned a
verdict, "Death from accidental drowning
by falling through the ice." 4 %, ~.

The funeral of Archbishop Hughes took

Ky, Bacon and Laughlin. Catholic clergy

diocese, and several of the adjacent States
The number of priests present was about
one hundred. The Sisters of Mercy and the
relatives of the deceased archbishop occll-
pied seats near the sanctuary. The clerical
procession, consisting of the bishops and
priests,w formed at 10 o'clock and marched
to the altar, where the solemn office for the
dead was chanted with fine effect After this
came Mozart's sublime requiem mass, sung
by choir selected from all the Catholic
churches i'll the city. The execution of the
mass both instrumental and vocal, was very
finished and effective. Rev. Bishop Nc.
Closky then delivered the funeral oratior
from the familiar text, 81 have fought Q
good fight" etc. 1t was an eloquent dis.
course, chiefly eulogistic of the Arch.
bishops religious character and history
The other ceremonies usual at Catholic
funerals followed, and the body was finally
placed in the vault of the building, where
it will probably remain until its removal tC
the new cathedral.


Flags throughout the city were displayed
at half mast in token of sorrow for the
event.

New YORK, Oct. lO.-The Worlds 10th
corps correspondence gives the following
account of the affair on Friday last:


The point at which the enemy first made
his appearance was near the intersection of
the DarbytOwn and White Tavern roads,
and was held by two brigades of cavalry,
| one OF which, under command OF Col. West,
was deplOyed across the Darbytown road
while the other, under Col. Spear, was de-
ployed parallel to it and across the White
Tavern road, covering the approach from
this direction. The enemy, when first seen,
was coming across the country from the
Charles City road, and moving towards the
right flank of Col West. The Col. changed
front hastily, SO as to form line parallel
with the road and facing the enemy. He
had hardly effected this and sheltered his
men behind low hedge skirting the road,
when the enemy in overwhelming numbers
dashed on him, and OH the command of Col.
Spear in almost simultaneous charges. The
men fired steadily, but could not stay the
rushing masses opposed to them.


1t was evident they must retreat, so the
command was given and they moved off
down the Darbytown road. Suddenly they
were checked in this direction, the enemy
having out6anked Spear, and had posses
sion of this avenue of retreat. AS there
was one more chance across the country,
they went around without organization.
The batteries of the 4th Division and lst u.
s., which fought bravely, moved off in the
same direction, taking blind wood road.
They had not gone far, however, when the
forward piece was mired. This stopped the
remainder, and on this spot they were cap
tured-eight guns in all-whcn the enemy,
who had followed closely, reached them
soon after. .-


The enemy having driven the cavalry
before them, now ceased the pursuit and
turned toward the unprotected flank of the
10th corps, which was held by the einvincble
old first, or Terry's division. The enemy,
flushed with his easily gained victory,
moved toward this little band with all the
confidence of victory. The brunt of his
attack was directed towards Abbott's sec
ond brigade. He might better have chosen
almost any other point, for half of these
troops being armed with repeating rifles,
made hasty records on the rebel ranks.
Moving towards them steadily, he exhibited
a determination to force the position
at any cost, but the unerring volcanic
tirearm of Abbott's brigade more than
equalized the game. Onward they pushed,
more dense grew the fire, still they ad-
vanced, until within about one hundred
PAGES of our crouching death dealers.
Then signs of weakness began to manifest
itself in their ranks, and they found that to
advance in the face of that fire was simply
marching to death. In short, there was
nothing for them but to slink away as best
they could, and stink away they did.


Not satisfied with the punishment he
inflicted, Terry at once prepared to follow
up his advantage. AS our lines approach
ed the enemy, it became evident that he
was Richmond bound, and the hopes of
overtaking him were fruitless. Still our
advance was pressed on until darkness in
terposed Then, just as Ponds brigade had
reached within half mile of the Darby
town road, the order was issued to return
within our dcfenses. In this advance we
picked up quite a number of prisoners,
stragglers, and men who waited behind to
desert. These, with our captures before
our works, swelled our list of captures to
some 200. Gen. Lee commanded in person,
and had evidently determined to make a
heavy impression.


Our loss in men has been very small, but
the enemy has suffered horribly. Their
prisoners report Gen. Gregg among their
killed. They brought two divisions into
action, one under Gen. Field, anda provis-
ional division under Hook.
